claims.statement: Susan B. Anthony was born on February 15, 1820, in Adams, Massachusetts, the second child of Daniel and Lucy Read Anthony.
Anthony voted in the 1872 presidential election, was arrested at her Rochester home, and was convicted at Canandaigua, New York; she refused to pay the $100 fine.

Her father, Daniel Anthony, who had not had a day's illness in forty years, was suddenly stricken in November 1862 with what was called acute neuralgia of the stomach and died two weeks later, on November 25, 1862, at 69.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary description from the authorized biography; the modern cause cannot be determined.

source_links.locator: Chapter on 1897: father died at sixty-nine

claims.statement: Her 1898 biography describes a long-lived family: her mother died at eighty-six, her paternal grandfather lived past ninety-seven, and both maternal grandparents died in their eighty-fourth year.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Causes of death are not recorded in the source.

claims.statement: In January 1891, after weeks of what seemed a persistent la grippe, Anthony collapsed at the Garrison home in Brookline, Massachusetts; pneumonia threatened and she kept to her room for a week.

On July 26, 1895, near the end of an address at Lakeside, Ohio, Anthony stopped abruptly and fainted; from July 30 she spent a month in bed with what was called nervous prostration, described as her first serious illness in seventy-five years.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The contemporary label does not establish a modern cause; no cardiac evaluation is recorded.

claims.statement: Her biographer described her daily habits in the late 1890s: a cold sponge bath each morning, simple food, tea and coffee in moderation, a rest after meals and an hour's rest each afternoon, and fresh air and exercise every day, walking from the station after a day on the train.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documents her baseline activity and habits; used for the synthetic social history.

claims.statement: In February 1906, although in failing health, Anthony traveled to Washington, D.C.; after returning to Rochester she went to bed, attended by Dr. Ricker and two nurses, and died about three weeks later.
Anthony died at her home on Madison Street in Rochester, New York, at 12:40 a.m. on March 13, 1906, aged 86; the National Park Service records the cause as heart failure and pneumonia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented anchor for the synthetic heart failure episode. Record the death as a fact without graphic detail.

hpi.narrative: Miss Anthony returns two weeks after starting furosemide and empagliflozin for newly diagnosed heart failure. She is less breathless and now climbs a flight of stairs with one pause instead of two. Her ankle swelling is gone by morning and returns only slightly in the evening. Her home weights have fallen steadily by about 1.7 kg. She has had no dizziness on standing, no excess thirst, and no genital itching or urinary symptoms since starting empagliflozin. She takes every dose and keeps a weight diary. Her echocardiogram and cardiology consultation were done this morning.

hpi.narrative: Miss Anthony is an 85-year-old woman with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (ejection fraction 62 percent) and hypertensive heart disease, euvolemic since June on as-needed furosemide, who asked for a same-day visit. Four days ago, two days after returning by train from a convention, she developed a runny nose and sore throat, followed by a dry cough that is worse at night and has woken her on two nights. Her sister had a cold the week before. A home COVID-19 antigen test on day two was negative. Her highest home temperature was 37.6 °C. Her daily weights have stayed between 56.0 and 56.4 kg, so she has not needed an extra furosemide dose. She is mildly breathless only during coughing fits, still sleeps on one pillow, and has kept walking, more slowly. Honey in hot tea eases the cough. She has taken nothing else, because the care plan told her to avoid cold remedies containing decongestants or ibuprofen.

Her one new concern is difficulty following questions from the back of crowded halls, more on the right.

referral.question: New heart failure in an active 85-year-old woman, likely with preserved ejection fraction. Please confirm the diagnosis, review the echocardiogram, and advise on any specific cause and on therapy
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks; echocardiogram booked for the same morning
referral.pertinent_history: Three months of breathlessness after one flight of stairs or a long station platform, with ankle swelling by evening and two-pillow orthopnea. NT-proBNP 1650 pg/mL; ECG shows sinus rhythm and left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage, without atrial fibrillation. Blood pressure 158/86 mmHg. Furosemide 20 mg and empagliflozin 10 mg were started today. Never smoker, no diabetes, kidney function near normal (eGFR 64)
questions: Does the echocardiogram confirm heart failure with preserved ejection fraction?
Is there any sign of a specific cause, such as cardiac amyloidosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or significant valve disease, that would change treatment?
Do you agree with adding spironolactone once potassium and kidney function are stable?
Is cardiac rehabilitation or any further testing worthwhile at her level of activity?

consultant_note.history: Miss Anthony is seen at the request of Dr. Pemberton two weeks after presenting with exertional breathlessness, orthopnea, and ankle swelling. On furosemide and empagliflozin she is already less breathless, and her home weight has fallen by about 1.7 kg. She has had no chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, numbness, or orthostatic lightheadedness. She lectures and travels most months and wants to keep doing so

assessment.display: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
assessment.assessment: Confirmed. Ejection fraction 62 percent with concentric remodeling, left atrial volume index 42 mL/m², and average E/e' 16 meet the diagnostic criteria with her raised NT-proBNP. Hypertension is the most likely cause

Cardiac amyloidosis is unlikely: septal thickness is only 11 mm, the ECG shows high rather than low voltage, and she has no carpal tunnel syndrome, neuropathy, or spinal stenosis. There is no hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or significant valve disease
Blood pressure 146/80 mmHg remains above the 130/80 target and is the main treatable driver

recommendations: Continue empagliflozin 10 mg daily long term
Start spironolactone 12.5 mg daily now; potassium 3.9 and eGFR 58 allow it. Check potassium and creatinine in one to two weeks
Continue furosemide 20 mg daily until euvolemic, then change to as-needed use guided by daily weights
No amyloid imaging or light-chain testing unless new red flags appear
No repeat echocardiogram unless her clinical status changes
Cardiac rehabilitation if her exercise tolerance plateaus; for now continue daily walking
